evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.
4. **What must remain my decision or another person’s responsibility?** Name the value judgment, permission or professional check that cannot be delegated.

artifactEvidence.excerpt: New York City announced on September 2 that its public schools would pause student-facing generative AI from early-childhood programs through eighth grade for the 2026–27 school year. The family notice said students would return September 10 under the new guidance. Student-facing means software a student directly uses. Generative AI creates text, images, audio or other content from instructions.

“Approved” also needs a boundary. NYC Public Schools says its current software-review process checks a tool’s privacy and security. The system says it is still building capacity to examine algorithmic bias, effects on equity and whether a tool actually helps instruction. Privacy approval therefore does not prove a pilot improves learning or is free of bias.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Why can a pilot tool be 'approved' by NYC Public Schools and still not be shown to help students learn or to be free of bias?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: Because the approval comes from ERMA, a review that currently checks only data privacy and security. It answers the question 'does this tool protect student data?' and nothing else. NYCPS itself says it is still building the capacity to evaluate algorithmic bias, equity effects and instructional effectiveness, so those questions simply have not been tested yet — approval proves what was reviewed, not everything a parent might hope it means.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Using this article's mechanism, what should the parent conclude from 'district-approved,' and what should they ask before signing?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: They should conclude only that the tool passed a data-privacy check — the specific question that vetting tested. It says nothing about whether the tutor's feedback is accurate, whether it treats students equitably, or whether it improves writing. Following the article's mechanism, the parent should ask three things: who will use the tool and for what (student practice, or anything touching grades or placement?), exactly what the approval review examined, and whether any evaluation of learning value or bias exists yet. The NYC policy itself doesn't apply in New Jersey, so the local district's own rules on staff decision-use also need asking.

sourceEvidence.excerpt: September 2, 2026

Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels today announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.

Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new text, images, audio, or other content in response to a user's instructions. These systems can produce inaccurate or biased information and can make it easier for students to bypass thinking they need to do themselves.
The student-facing restrictions described on this page apply specifically to generative AI.

For the 2026-27 school year, New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in grades 2K–8, with limited use in high schools, and screen time restrictions depending on grade.
Software that uses student-facing generative AI is not permitted in grades 2K–8.

Five pilots have been centrally approved for grades 9–12 (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools). Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots, and each application will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Regarding individual student exposure to AI, we will ensure that students are participating in only one pilot.

Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time, provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan. Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to other necessary tools.

Teachers and other school staff members may continue using AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, subject to existing requirements, including the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security approval process, and NYCPS procurement rules. Additionally, AI may not be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. All special education documents are developed by qualified professionals; counseling, crisis intervention, and therapeutic support are provided only by qualified staff members.

The ERMA process currently reviews tools for data privacy and security. NYCPS is committed to building expanded evaluation capacity, including areas not covered by ERMA such as algorithmic bias, equity impact, and instructional effectiveness.

For AI tools being used in your child's school, contact your school principal. For concerns, you can contact your child's school, the School Leadership Team (SLT) or your Community Education Council (CEC).

While public feedback survey is now closed, you can share feedback directly to your school, participate in your school's PTA, attend your local Community Education Council events, or the Panel for Educational Policy.

The Technology in Schools Coalition, comprised of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners, and experts in the field, will provide recommendations on the future of technology use in NYCPS classrooms and will deliver a report of policy recommendations in April 2027.

New York City’s public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen time limits but said the city’s AI policy “leaves many questions unanswered,” including how the Education Department “will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards.”

Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year. “A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time,” he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms “to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they’re safe, that they’re not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they’re not leading to rampant cheating.”

sourceEvidence.excerpt: New York City’s public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen time limits but said the city’s AI policy “leaves many questions unanswered,” including how the Education Department “will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards.”

Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year. “A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time,” he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms “to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they’re safe, that they’re not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they’re not leading to rampant cheating.”

sourceEvidence.excerpt: Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new text, images, audio, or other content in response to a user's instructions. These systems can produce inaccurate or biased information and can make it easier for students to bypass thinking they need to do themselves.
The student-facing restrictions described on this page apply specifically to generative AI.

For the 2026-27 school year, New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in grades 2K–8, with limited use in high schools, and screen time restrictions depending on grade.
Software that uses student-facing generative AI is not permitted in grades 2K–8.

Five pilots have been centrally approved for grades 9–12 (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools). Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots, and each application will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Regarding individual student exposure to AI, we will ensure that students are participating in only one pilot.

Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time, provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan. Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to other necessary tools.

Teachers and other school staff members may continue using AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, subject to existing requirements, including the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security approval process, and NYCPS procurement rules. Additionally, AI may not be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. All special education documents are developed by qualified professionals; counseling, crisis intervention, and therapeutic support are provided only by qualified staff members.

The ERMA process currently reviews tools for data privacy and security. NYCPS is committed to building expanded evaluation capacity, including areas not covered by ERMA such as algorithmic bias, equity impact, and instructional effectiveness.
